X/Twitter and Telegram alpha as a tradab.topic: X/Twitter and Telegram alpha as a tradable signal for Solana memecoin trading — 2026 ingestion economics and whether the signal is real
X/Twitter and Telegram alpha as a tradab.executive_summary:
INGESTION (a): X's official API moved to pure pay-per-usage in 2026 — $0.005 per Post read, $0.010 per User read, hard-capped at 3,000,000 Post reads/month before Enterprise (docs.x.com, verbatim). Filtered Stream IS available on pay-per-use (1 connection, 1,000 rules, 1,024-char rules, 250 posts/sec, ~6-7s P99 latency); the sub-second product (Powerstream) is Enterprise-only. Every delivered stream Post is billed at $0.005, so a broad CA-matching rule is financially ruinous. Resources are deduplicated within a 24h UTC window, which is the single biggest cost lever. Third parties are 30-250x cheaper: Sorsa (ex-TweetScout domain) $49/mo for 10K requests at 20 req/s; twitterapi.io $0.15/1K tweets, QPS tiered by credit balance (3/6/10/20); SocialData $0.0002/item, 120 req/min, plus a webhook Monitoring API at ~$5/monitor/month with explicitly non-real-time ~30s delivery; Apify actors $0.15-$0.40/1K tweets. Nitter's public-instance model is dead (real accounts/session tokens now required); twscrape works but needs your own X account pool. Kaito's formerly-free Yaps endpoint now returns Unauthorized and its Open Protocol doc page 404s. Elfa AI is the only vendor I verified that ships trending *contract addresses* by mention count for both Twitter and Telegram (free tier 1,000 credits/mo, 60 RPM; Grow $290/mo, 40K credits, 120 RPM; PAYG/x402 $0.009/credit, x402 at 1,000 RPM). LunarCrush Individual is $90/mo but only 10 req/min and 2,000 req/day — arithmetically incapable of per-launch polling. Santiment gates real-time API behind Sanbase Max $249/mo (Pro's API data carries a 30-day lag). Moby's moby.trade domain has expired; Alphanomics is showing a maintenance page; ChainEdge publishes no pricing page. For Telegram, Telethon over MTProto is free, sub-second, and the only retail-cost social feed fast enough to matter — but one account can join at most 500 channels/supergroups (1,000 with Premium), which is the real capacity constraint.

DOES IT WORK (b): The measured literature is uniformly hostile to buying at the call. Dhawan & Putniņš (355 pumps) find participants join "despite negative expected returns" with 65% average price distortion. Xu & Livshits (412 Telegram pumps) estimate admins netted 199.52 BTC (~$1.1M) across 348 events at an aggregate 18% insider return, and document a channel that announced the coin *when the price was already at its peak*, making follower profit arithmetically impossible; they also find views-vs-pump-gain correlation of −0.162, i.e. bigger channel does not mean bigger pump. La Morgia et al. show ranked/VIP members receive the signal 1-10 seconds ahead of ordinary members and that abnormal *sell* volume appears at second 19 of the pump — the dump begins while followers are still buying. Clough & Edwards (10,687 events, 765 coins) measure peak at roughly two minutes, average 5-minute max gain of 15.02% on Binance-class venues vs 790.54% on illiquid ones, and −30% relative price one year later. On Solana specifically: the strongest published social result is that advertising a Telegram channel in pump.fun launch metadata raises the fast-regime graduation rate from 0.166% to 1.485% (8.94x, Cox HR 5.40, n=832,941) while advertising a Twitter account barely moves it (0.1486% → 0.2268%, HR 1.30). Both of the best-performing published Solana rug/risk models (MELT, "Catching the Rug", 6.4M tokens) use zero social features — on-chain behavior alone. No published work I could find establishes predictive value for "first mention velocity" on memecoins; the closest honest evidence (Alizadeh et al.) finds a ≥6-hour lag on majors only, and the YouTube finfluencer study finds aggregate video counts Granger-cause price but *top* finfluencers' videos do not. Coordinated bot amplification is real and measurable: 61% of accounts retweeting NFT promotion tweets were bot-like at Botometer t=0.43, and 36% of promoted projects were fraudulent — but Botometer itself is no longer usable, so you must build your own classifier. Verdict: X mention data is a *disqualifier* feature (fake-account detection, bot-amplification detection), not an entry trigger. Telegram presence in launch metadata is a legitimate weak prior. Paid "KOL alpha" products sold to retail are, as far as published measurement goes, unverified marketing.

findings.claim: X API v2 in 2026 is pay-per-usage only; there are no published subscription tiers on the official docs
findings.detail: docs.x.com/x-api/getting-started/pricing states verbatim: 'The X API uses pay-per-usage pricing. No subscriptions—pay only for what you use.' Read prices per resource returned: Posts $0.005, User $0.010, DM Event $0.010, Following/Followers $0.010, List $0.005, Space $0.005, Like/Mute/Block $0.001. Writes per request: Post:Create $0.015, Post:Create(with URL) $0.200, Trends $0.010, Counts:Recent $0.005, Counts:All $0.010. Webhook events billed per delivered event (post.create $0.005). 'Owned Reads' (your own app's own data) are $0.001/resource. Third-party blogs (twitterapi.io, xpoz, socialcrawl) claim legacy Basic $200/mo and Pro $5,000/mo still exist for grandfathered subscribers and that new signups cannot buy them — that claim does NOT appear on the official docs and should be treated as unverified.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Budget in per-resource units, not seats. A per-launch social check of 1 profile + 20 mentions costs $0.010 + $0.100 = $0.11 on the official API. At 200 qualifying launches/day that is $22/day / ~$660/mo — 30x what twitterapi.io or SocialData cost for identical data.

findings.claim: The pay-per-usage plan is capped at 3,000,000 Post reads per monthly billing cycle, not 2,000,000
findings.detail: Official docs note, verbatim: 'Pay-per-usage plans are capped at 3 million Post reads per monthly billing cycle. If you need higher volume, upgrade to an Enterprise plan.' At $0.005/read that is a $15,000/month ceiling. Multiple 2026 blog posts state a 2,000,000 cap (~$10,000/mo) — those are stale or wrong. Enterprise pricing is not published anywhere official; the widely-repeated '~$42,000/month' figure is third-party hearsay and I found no primary source for it.
findings.actionable_for_bot: You will never approach 3M reads if you gate reads behind the on-chain filter. Treat the cap as a non-issue and the '$42K enterprise' number as unverifiable marketing folklore when someone quotes it at you.

findings.claim: Resources are deduplicated within a 24-hour UTC window — re-reading the same Post or user the same day is free
findings.detail: Verbatim: 'All resources are deduplicated within a 24-hour UTC day window... requesting the same resource again within that window will not incur an additional charge... The deduplication window resets at midnight UTC.' Marked a 'soft guarantee' with outage edge cases.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Poll the same KOL profile or the same mention set as often as you like within a UTC day at zero marginal cost. Structure any monitoring loop to re-read rather than to search-with-new-parameters, since new parameters return new (billable) resources.

findings.claim: Filtered Stream IS available on pay-per-use in 2026, with ~6-7 second P99 latency; the low-latency product is Enterprise-gated
findings.detail: docs.x.com/x-api/posts/filtered-stream/introduction, access-levels table: Pay-per-use gets 1,000 rules per project, 1,024-char rules, 1 connection, core operators; Enterprise gets 25,000+ rules, 2,048 chars, multiple connections, and the semantic 'embedding:' operator. Verbatim note: 'Filtered Stream prioritizes data hydration and delivery, with approximately 6-7 seconds of P99 latency.' Keep-alive is a blank line every 20 seconds; reconnect if nothing arrives for 20s. Powerstream (docs.x.com/x-api/powerstream/introduction) is the low-latency alternative — 1,000 rules, 2,048 chars, local-datacenter option — and is verbatim 'a premium offering available under select Enterprise plans.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: 6-7s P99 is 16-19 Solana slots (I measured 359-375 ms/slot live on mainnet-beta via getRecentPerformanceSamples). Anyone with a scraping path or an Enterprise Powerstream feed acts before you. Do not architect an entry trigger on Filtered Stream; use it for post-hoc labelling and disqualification.

findings.claim: Exact X API rate limits per endpoint (2026)
findings.detail: From docs.x.com/x-api/fundamentals/rate-limits: GET /2/tweets/search/recent 450/15min per app, 300/15min per user, 100 max results, 512-char query, last 7 days, available to all developers. GET /2/tweets/search/all 1/sec and 300/15min per app, 500 max results, 1,024-char query, back to March 2006, 'available to pay-per-use and Enterprise customers'. GET /2/tweets/search/stream 50/15min, 1 connection, 1,000 rules, 250 posts/sec. POST /2/tweets/search/stream/rules 100/15min. GET /2/users/by/username/:username 300/15min per app. GET /2/users/:id/followers 300/15min. GET /2/tweets 3,500/15min per app. Headers: x-rate-limit-limit / -remaining / -reset.
findings.actionable_for_bot: 300 user lookups per 15 min = 1,200/hour is your hard ceiling for account-age checks on the official API. Sorsa's 20 req/s (72,000/hour) or twitterapi.io's 20 QPS at 50,000+ credits are ~60x more headroom for the same job.

findings.claim: twitterapi.io: $0.15/1K tweets, $0.18/1K users, QPS gated by credit balance
findings.detail: Pricing page: 'Tweets: $0.15 per 1K tweets', 'Profiles: $0.18 per 1K users', 'Followers/Following: from $0.01 per 1K, tiered', 'Follower IDs: from $0.0045 per 1K, tiered'. '1 USD = 100,000 Credits'. 'Minimum $0.00015 (15 Credits) per API call'. 'Pay as you go, no minimum spend required'; 'Recharged credits never expire'; bonus credits valid 30 days. /qps-limits page: free users 1 request per 5 seconds; paid QPS by balance — 1,000+ credits = 3 QPS, 5,000+ = 6 QPS, 10,000+ = 10 QPS, 50,000+ = 20 QPS. 75+ endpoints claimed.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Cheapest verified per-tweet rate. Note the QPS ladder is balance-gated, not plan-gated: park $500 (50,000 credits) to unlock 20 QPS. Per-launch check (1 profile + 20 mentions) ≈ $0.0032; 200 launches/day ≈ $19/month.

findings.claim: SocialData.tools: $0.0002 per item, 120 req/min shared across all endpoints, plus a webhook Monitoring API
findings.detail: docs.socialdata.tools/getting-started/pricing: 'Most of our endpoints follow the same pricing structure - $0.0002 per tweet or user profile returned (or $0.2 per 1000 items)'; failed requests are not billed; HTTP 402 when balance is zero. Rate limits page: '120 requests per minute' per API key, shared across endpoints; higher limits free on request. Monitoring API pricing: User monitors billed hourly with volume tiers — 1-10 monitors $0.0069/hr (~$4.99/mo), 11-100 $0.0062/hr (~$4.49/mo), 101-300 $0.0055/hr (~$3.99/mo), 301-500 $0.0048/hr, 501-1000 $0.0042/hr, 1000+ $0.0035/hr (~$2.49/mo). Search monitors: '$0.0002 per tweet delivered' plus '$0.0002 flat, for every execution that delivers nothing'; at 30-second refresh that is 2,880 executions/day = $0.58/day = ~$17.28/mo minimum per search monitor. Monitor types: user tweets, user following, user profile, search.
findings.actionable_for_bot: The 'user profile' monitor is the single most valuable primitive in this whole document for your use case: it fires a webhook when a monitored account's bio or display name changes — which is exactly the repurposed/hacked-account signature. At ~$4.99/mo for 10 monitors you can watch a curated KOL set cheaply.

findings.claim: SocialData explicitly disclaims real-time delivery: ~30 seconds typical
findings.detail: docs.socialdata.tools/monitoring/introduction: 'We do not promise real-time delivery'; events 'typically arrive within 30 seconds'; the docs explicitly recommend against building systems requiring sub-second responsiveness. Monitors capture only future activity — 'Creating a monitor establishes a baseline from the current state'. Events are deduplicated; monitors pause when balance depletes and auto-resume.
findings.actionable_for_bot: 30 seconds is ~80 Solana slots. This is a labelling/enrichment feed, categorically not an entry trigger. Your existing 60-300s participation-evidence wait is actually well matched to this latency — feed the webhook into the scoring model, not into an order.

findings.claim: Sorsa (serving the tweetscout.io domain) — flat per-request X API alternative with crypto-specific scoring endpoints
findings.detail: api.sorsa.io: base URL https://api.sorsa.io/v3, auth header 'ApiKey: YOUR_API_KEY', 40 endpoints, 20 req/sec on every plan, claimed 300ms p50, 100 free requests on signup. Plans: Starter 10K req/mo $49, Pro 100K req/mo $199, Enterprise 500K req/mo $899; 'from $0.02 per 1K tweets', 'from $0.01 per 1K profiles', verification checks 'from $0.002 per check'. Crypto section (Section 7, backed by an internal crypto-account database, explicitly not full X coverage): GET /score (numeric crypto influence score), GET /score-changes (7d/30d delta), GET /followers-stats (breakdown into influencers/projects/VCs counts), GET /top-followers, GET /top-following, GET /new-followers-7d, GET /new-following-7d. Section 8: GET /username-to-id/{handle} — 'Unlike usernames, user IDs never change.' The User model returns created_at (ISO 8601 account creation date), followers_count, tweets_count, bio_urls, verified.
findings.actionable_for_bot: This is the best-fit single vendor: it gives you created_at + stable user_id + a crypto-native influence score + follower-composition in one API at 20 req/s. /followers-stats returning near-zero influencers/projects/VCs on an account with a large raw follower count is a direct purchased-followers tell.

findings.claim: Elfa AI is the only verified vendor exposing trending contract addresses by social mention count for BOTH Twitter and Telegram
findings.detail: GET /v2/aggregations/trending-cas/twitter and GET /v2/aggregations/trending-cas/telegram — 'Get trending contract addresses mentioned on Twitter/X. Returns contract addresses with mention counts', 'Plan Access: All plans (Free and above)', 'Data Recency: Computed at ingest in real time', 'Rate Limit 60 to 120 RPM by plan'. Takes either timeWindow or from/to. Other relevant endpoints: GET /v2/account/smart-stats (marked experimental), GET /v2/data/keyword-mentions (cursor-paginated, metadata.total capped at 10000, returns repostBreakdown.smart and repostBreakdown.ct = reposts by 'smart' and 'crypto-Twitter' accounts, no raw tweet text — only a link field), GET /v2/data/top-mentions, GET /v2/aggregations/trending-tokens. Pricing: Free $0/1,000 credits/60 RPM; Grow $290/mo ($2,958/yr) 40,000 credits 120 RPM; PAYG $0.009/credit, $20 minimum top-up, 60 RPM; x402 $0.009/credit paid in USDC on Base/Arbitrum/Polygon/Avalanche/Solana, no account, 1,000 RPM. Auth header 'x-elfa-api-key'. Every /v2/* response carries an 'x-elfa-credits' header with the exact cost. Event-summary and trending-narratives endpoints cost 5 credits each.
findings.actionable_for_bot: trending-cas/telegram at 1,000 RPM via x402 is the cheapest way to get a mention-count time series keyed by contract address without building Telethon infrastructure. repostBreakdown.smart vs repostBreakdown.ct is a ready-made coordinated-amplification ratio: high ct, near-zero smart = shill farm.

findings.claim: LunarCrush's rate limits make per-launch use arithmetically impossible on the cheaper plans
findings.detail: Pricing page: Individual $90/mo ($72/mo annual), Builder $300/mo ($240 annual), Scale $900/mo ($720 annual), Enterprise custom. Rate limits by plan: Hobby 4 req/min and 100 req/day; Individual 10 req/min and 2,000 req/day; Builder 100 req/min and 20,000 req/day; Scale 500 req/min and 100,000 req/day. Base URL under lunarcrush.com/api4/public/, auth 'Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>'. Hobby is market-data only; 'social, creator, and AI endpoints unlock on paid plans.' Coverage is a curated coin/topic universe (Galaxy Score, AltRank), not arbitrary Solana mints.
findings.actionable_for_bot: 2,000 requests/day at Individual is ~1.4 req/min sustained. If you see 1,000+ launches/day you cannot even do one call per launch. LunarCrush is a majors/narrative tool; it will not have your 90-second-old mint in coverage at all. Skip it for this bot.

findings.claim: Santiment's real-time API is gated behind the $249/mo tier; the $49 tier's API data is deliberately 30 days stale
findings.detail: app.santiment.net/pricing: Free — '1K API calls / mo, 1 year historical data', 'Real-time API data with 30-day lag'. Sanbase Pro $49/mo ($529/yr) — '5K API calls / mo', still 'Real-time API data with 30-day lag'. Sanbase Max $249/mo ($2,700/yr) — 'Real-time API data without restrictions', '80K API calls / mo, 2 years historical data'. Social volume metric (academy.santiment.net/metrics/social-volume/): 'The total number of social data text documents that contain the given search term at least once', sources = Telegram, Twitter, Reddit, 4chan, BitcoinTalk, YouTube videos; five-minute update intervals; supports arbitrary Lucene search terms, not just covered assets; historical data can be recalculated for the previous month when labels or sources change.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Only Max ($249/mo, 80K calls) is usable live, and 80K calls/mo = 2,666/day. The arbitrary-Lucene-search-term capability means you could query a raw contract address as the search term — but 5-minute granularity plus the 80K cap makes this a research tool, not a live feed. The 'previous month recalculation' clause means any backtest you build on it is not reproducible.

findings.claim: Kaito's Yaps public API is no longer free/open — it now returns Unauthorized and its Open Protocol documentation page 404s
findings.detail: I called https://api.kaito.ai/api/v1/yaps?username=elonmusk directly: response body {"message":"Unauthorized"}. https://docs.kaito.ai/kaito-yaps-tokenized-attention/yaps-open-protocol returns HTTP 404. Kaito Pro pricing (pro.kaito.ai/pricing) now shows only 'Enterprise Single-Seat $833/month billed annually' with API access as 'Contact Sales'. Search results indicate the Yaps post-to-earn program was sunset in January 2026 and the older documented default rate limit was 100 calls per 5 minutes.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Any tutorial or repo that hits the unauthenticated Yaps endpoint is dead code. Do not plan around Kaito mindshare unless you are prepared to talk to sales at $833/seat/month equivalent. There is no published evidence that yaps or mindshare predicts memecoin returns.

findings.claim: Apify's X scraper actors are 3-13x more expensive per tweet than the pure API vendors
findings.detail: apidojo/tweet-scraper ('Tweet Scraper V2'): 'Pricing from $0.40 / 1,000 tweets', claimed 30-80 tweets per second, 7.3K monthly active users, rating 3.9 from 196 reviews, community-maintained (not Apify-official). A cheaper competing actor, scrape.badger/twitter-tweets-scraper, advertises '$0.15 per 1,000 results' with 40+ search filters and no API key needed.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Apify adds an actor-run orchestration layer you do not need for a low-latency loop. Use it only for bulk historical backfill of KOL timelines when building your labelled call dataset; use twitterapi.io or Sorsa for the live path.

findings.claim: Nitter's free public-instance model is dead but the project is not archived; twscrape is the viable self-hosted path and requires your own X account pool
findings.detail: github.com/zedeus/nitter README (not archived, 1,336 commits): 'Running a Nitter instance now requires real accounts, since Twitter removed the previous methods.' Session tokens must be obtained per the wiki. github.com/vladkens/twscrape (~2.7k stars, 288 commits): 'an async Python library and CLI for X/Twitter Search and GraphQL endpoints. It runs on your own account pool, keeps sessions in SQLite, rotates accounts when an endpoint is rate-limited'. Auth via browser cookies (auth_token + ct0) or username/password with email verification. 'Rate limits are tracked per account and per endpoint. When an account is limited for one operation, twscrape locks it for that operation until the reset time and tries another active account.' Reporting from 2024-2026 states guest tokens expired in February 2024 and, as of January 2025, guest tokens were bound to browser fingerprints with datacenter IPs permanently banned.
findings.actionable_for_bot: twscrape's real cost is account attrition and residential proxies, not software. Budget for a rotating pool and expect periodic total breakage when X changes GraphQL. For a production trading bot, the $19-49/month you save over twitterapi.io is not worth the outage risk on a component you cannot fix at 3am.

findings.claim: Telegram via Telethon/MTProto is the only sub-second social feed available at retail cost — but one account caps at 500 channels
findings.detail: limits.tginfo.me: 'Channels and supergroups number you can be member of (combined): up to 500 (including ones you own)' — 'up to 1000' with Premium. Group/channel creation limited to 50/day. Official clients allow up to 3 accounts (4-6 on some apps). Supergroups support up to 200,000 members; broadcast channels are unlimited. Telethon's Message object exposes id, date (UTC), message text, entities, views (broadcast channel view count), forwards, edit_date, reply_to. events.NewMessage delivers over the persistent MTProto connection with no polling interval. TGStat, which indexes 2,832,100 channels and 63.37bn posts, claims new posts appear in search 'as soon as in 7 seconds after being posted' — that is the third-party-index floor, versus sub-second for a direct MTProto subscription.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Design for N accounts × 500 channels. Two accounts at 500 each covers 1,000 channels for the cost of two SIMs. Message.views and Message.forwards give you a free, per-call reach measurement that no X product gives you cheaply. Note edit_date: call channels edit messages to change the CA — always store the original text and diff on edit.

findings.claim: The largest 'crypto' Telegram channels are airdrop/tap-to-earn farms, not call channels — channel-size rankings are useless for finding callers
findings.detail: TGStat's crypto channel rating by subscribers is topped by Blum (@blumcrypto) 15,288,096; Major Community (@majors) 11,754,854; Catapult Extreme (@catapult_extreme) 9,022,056; Roxman (@roxman) 7,614,208; DOGS Community (@dogs) 7,385,407; FX Holding (@fx_holding_community) 6,422,996; Time Farm News (@TimeFarmChannel) 5,604,564; Tofan Trade (@Tofan_Trade) 5,230,803; Tonkeeper News (@tonkeeper_news) 5,007,986; Bitget Wallet Announcements 4,210,268. None of these are Solana memecoin call channels. I probed plausible handles (@pumpfunalerts=129 subscribers, @potionalpha=34, @solanagems=91 members) and found no large public Solana call channel by guessing — the real ones are private, invite-gated, or rotate handles.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not build a channel list from public rankings. Build it from the launch side: parse the telegram field in pump.fun launch metadata, resolve each t.me link, and score channels by realised forward performance of the CAs they posted. That is a self-bootstrapping, objective discovery mechanism and it is the only honest one.

findings.claim: TGStat is a usable Telegram-wide index with published pricing, ~7s indexing latency
findings.detail: 2,832,100 channels, 286,300 groups, 63.37bn posts, +33.7m new posts in 24 hours. 'New posts are indexed in real-time and are present in search results as soon as in 7 seconds after being posted on Telegram.' Pricing: Free — 20 recent posts per search, 7-day result window. Personal — 2,940 RUB/month, 1,000 posts per search, group searching, all filters. Corporate — 6,300 RUB/month, up to 5 accounts. Offers an API for statistics and post search plus a callback API.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Useful for retrospective 'who posted this CA first and when' across 2.8M channels, which you cannot do with Telethon (you only see channels you joined). The 7s index latency rules it out as a trigger. api.tgstat.org did not resolve DNS from this environment — verify the API host before depending on it.

findings.claim: Moby is effectively gone and Alphanomics is down; ChainEdge publishes no pricing
findings.detail: moby.trade returns a Namecheap 'Domain registration has expired' page. www.mobyagent.com returns HTTP 200 but renders empty (JS shell, no content). alphanomics.io returns 'We'll be back soon — We're making improvements.' chainedge.io loads a smart-money-wallet-tracking marketing site but /pricing and /pricing/ both 404. I found no public API documentation, endpoint, or price for any of the three, and no Phantom-hosted Moby API.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Treat all three as non-integrable. Anyone citing 'Moby alpha' or 'Alphanomics signals' in 2026 is quoting a dead or undocumented product.

findings.claim: Followers who buy at the call face NEGATIVE expected returns — this is the headline peer-reviewed finding, not a caveat
findings.detail: Dhawan & Putniņš, 'A New Wolf in Town? Pump-and-Dump Manipulation in Cryptocurrency Markets' (SSRN 3670714, published in Review of Finance): 'We investigate the puzzle of widespread participation in cryptocurrency pump-and-dump manipulation schemes... Puzzlingly, people join in despite negative expected returns... Analyzing a sample of 355 cases in six months, we find strong empirical support for both mechanisms [overconfidence and gambling preferences]. Pumps generate extreme price distortions of 65% on average, abnormal trading volumes in the millions of dollars, and large wealth transfers between participants.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: The academic consensus is that the call is the exit liquidity event, not the entry. Any strategy whose entry condition is 'a call happened' is, per the only large-sample study that computes it, negative-EV before fees and slippage. If you use call data at all, use it as a feature that must be combined with a pre-call on-chain edge, or as a veto.

findings.claim: Insiders capture ~18% aggregate return; at least one channel announced the coin when price was already at peak, making follower profit impossible
findings.detail: Xu & Livshits (USENIX Security 2019, arXiv:1811.10109), 412 pump-and-dumps across 300+ Telegram channels, 2018-06-17 to 2019-02-26. Table 1 (348 events with price data): Binance 51 events / 148.97 BTC admin profit / 15% admin return; Bittrex 15 / 0.92 / 7%; Cryptopia 180 / 44.09 / 57%; Yobit 102 / 5.54 / 52%; Total 348 / 199.52 BTC / 18%. Verbatim: 'We estimate that admins made a net proﬁt of 199.52 BTC, equivalent to 1.1 million USD, through 348 pump and dump events'; 'Since trading is a zero-sum game, the aggregate investor loss would be on the equivalent scale as the aggregate admin win.' Case study: 'Bomba bitcoin "cryptopia" only announced the coin at the time when the coin price was already at its peak, making it impossible for investors who solely relied on the channel to make any money.' Also: 'Three and half minutes after the start of the pump-and-dump, the coin price had dropped below its open price.' And on Cryptopia: 'in numerous pumps, coin prices were elevated to such an extent that the hourly return before the pump even exceeds the hourly return during the pump' — i.e. organisers front-run their own announcement.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Pre-announcement price/volume drift is measurable and is your only realistic edge in this data — if you can detect accumulation BEFORE the call, that is a signal; the call itself is the top. The 3.5-minute round trip to below open sets your maximum tolerable holding period if you ever do trade a call.

findings.claim: Channel reach is NEGATIVELY correlated with pump gain (-0.162) — bigger channel does not mean bigger move
findings.detail: Xu & Livshits: 'we ﬁnd a negative correlation (-0.162) between number of views of coin announcement and pump gain, which is rather counter-intuitive... Two extreme examples: the coin announcement of the pump on MST had 325 views and the pump gain was 12.6%; another coin announcement of the pump on PARTY had only 18 views, and the pump gain was a whopping 533.3%. This ﬁnding suggests that the number of views cannot accurately proxy number of participants.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not weight a call by follower count or view count. If you build a channel-quality score, weight by realised forward return of the CAs the channel posted, not by audience size. This single finding invalidates most retail 'follow the big KOLs' products.

findings.claim: The dump begins ~19 seconds into the pump, and tiered channels give VIPs a 1-10 second head start
findings.detail: La Morgia, Mei, Sassi, Stefa — 'Pump and Dumps in the Bitcoin Era' (arXiv:2005.06610) and 'The Doge of Wall Street' (arXiv:2105.00733, ACM TOIT), ~900 events over 3+ years across 20 Telegram groups. On the OAX pump: 'there are two buy peaks... of approximately 65 Bitcoins' and 'a peak in the sell volumes of almost 10 Bitcoins at the moment of the first buy peak, the 19th second. Considering that group members are still buying and the reaction time for outsiders is too short, this sudden big sell volume is abnormal. There can be only two possible actors to sell their assets: the bots and the admins.' On tiering: 'The advantage in terms of time of being at a higher level is usually between 0.5 and 1 second with respect to the next level, and the maximum advantage is in the interval between 1 and 10 seconds.' Big Pump Signal peaked at 200,000 Telegram members and 250,000 Discord members. Their real-time detector fires within 25 seconds (F1 94.5%) vs 30 minutes for the Kamps & Kleinberg baseline (F1 62.7%).
findings.actionable_for_bot: If a channel is tiered, you are structurally in the last cohort. Quantify it: measure the timestamp gap between the earliest on-chain buy of a CA and the channel message timestamp. If median gap > 0 (buys precede the post), that channel is front-run and its calls are unusable. This is a cheap, objective per-channel test you can run on your own data.

findings.claim: Pump price peaks in roughly two minutes; average 5-minute max gain is 15% on liquid venues vs 790% on illiquid ones; -30% one year later
findings.detail: Clough & Edwards, 'Pump, Dump, and then What?' (arXiv:2309.06608, APWG eCrime 2023). Dataset expanded from 1,111 to 10,687 pump events across 765 coins. Verbatim: 'the price rapidly rises as participants buy into the coin, peaks for around two minutes, then rapidly falls'. ΔP is defined as (Pmax − Pbefore)/Pbefore over 'the maximum price in the 5 minutes after a pump announcement'. 'The maximum price increase, on average, is much lower (15.02% vs 790.54%) for pumps organised by CPI and therefore for those taking place on Binance.' Long-run: 'the long-term impact of pump and dump schemes on the targeted assets is negative, amounting to an average 30% relative drop in price a year after the pump event.' Most-targeted coin: 98 pumps over 4 years. Prior work cited: Victor & Hagermann found a pumped coin performs ~10% better than peers over 100 days (contradicting the -30% figure); Aggarwal-style equity manipulation studies show peak CAR 28% decaying to 0% by day +100.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Two-minute peak sets the entire trade clock. The 15% vs 790% split is the key structural insight: gains scale inversely with liquidity, which is exactly why your 2%-of-pool-depth sizing cap is the right constraint — the venues where calls produce big prints are the venues where you cannot get size out.

findings.claim: On pump.fun, an advertised Telegram channel is a strong graduation predictor; an advertised Twitter account is nearly worthless
findings.detail: Kamat, 'Pump.fun Graduation Regime Windows' (arXiv:2607.02823v3), 832,941 launches, 1,651 graduations, 2026-05-08 to 2026-06-10. Stratified fast-regime graduation rates: has_twitter=0 n=304,815, 453 grads, 0.1486% [0.136, 0.163]; has_twitter=1 n=528,126, 1,198 grads, 0.2268% [0.214, 0.240]; log-rank p=1.1e-14. has_website=0 0.1584%, has_website=1 0.2636%, p=1.2e-25. has_telegram=0 n=812,671, 0.1661%; has_telegram=1 n=20,270, 1.4850% [1.327, 1.661], p<1e-300, an 8.94x lift. Multivariate Cox: has_telegram HR 5.402 [4.733, 6.166]; log(1+mcap_sol) HR 4.506; has_twitter HR 1.305 [1.192, 1.428]; has_website HR 1.194; log(1+desc_len) HR 1.054. Concordance 0.858. By social_count: 0 channels (n=267,322) 0.1104%; 1 (n=281,289) 0.2293%; 2 (n=270,622) 0.1655%; 3 (n=13,708) 1.9186% — a 17.4x lift for full stack over none, but NON-MONOTONIC (2 is worse than 1), so essentially all the signal is the Telegram indicator. CRITICAL CAVEAT the author documents in full: the collector polled a top-50-newest endpoint and effectively only observed ~6 minutes post-launch, so all rates are fast-regime lower bounds, not 24-hour rates; a later attempted correction was tested on-chain (0 of 100 sampled mints confirmed) and withdrawn.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Add has_telegram from launch metadata as a scoring feature with roughly an 8-9x prior lift — it is free, available at mint, and it is the single strongest social variable published. Do NOT add has_twitter as a positive: HR 1.30 with 63% of all launches carrying one means it discriminates almost nothing. Only 2.43% of launches (20,270/832,941) advertise Telegram, so this gates you to a small, high-prior subset — exactly the shape you want given your 7.5%-ever-2x base rate.

findings.claim: The best published Solana memecoin risk models use ZERO social features
findings.detail: I grep-searched the full text of both for 'twitter', 'telegram', and 'social media' and found zero occurrences. MELT (arXiv:2602.13480, Georgia Tech): 41k+ Solana memecoin launches, 200M+ transactions, 122 behavioral features, all on-chain; finds 'on average, 36.5% of token supply is held by coordinated accounts'; integrating model predictions into a selection strategy 'reduces investment loss significantly'. 'Catching the Rug' (arXiv:2608.20271): 6.4 million Solana tokens over 7 months; 'a vast majority of these memecoins exhibit rug pull characteristics within one hour of launch'; XGBoost achieves robust detection 'using only the first 5 minutes of trading data'; cross-platform generalization tested between PumpFun and Raydium with multi-source fusion mitigating domain shift.
findings.actionable_for_bot: This is the blunt answer to 'is social alpha real for memecoins': the published state of the art beats the problem without touching X or Telegram at all. Your on-chain filter stack is the load-bearing component. Social data should be additive at the margin (Telegram-presence prior, hacked-account veto, bot-amplification veto) and should never be allowed to override an on-chain reject.

findings.claim: Coordinated sniper wallet rings measurably lift early buyer flow but not SOL inflow — the 'crowd' they appear to summon is largely themselves
findings.detail: Kamat, 'Coordinated Sniper Cohorts on Pump.fun' (arXiv:2607.02795v3): 1,578,333 buyer observations across 166,098 launches over 13.38 days. Union-find on co-occurrence graphs identifies 1,012 persistent wallet cohorts (2-12 wallets each, 2,965 unique addresses). Contamination-adjusted 1:1 propensity-score matching (0.2-SD caliper, 10 covariates, 5,419 matched pairs, worst post-match SMD 0.077) gives first-30-minute buyer-count lift +16.1% [+13.0%, +19.4%], but first-30-minute SOL-inflow lift +6.3% [−0.5%, +15.1%] — NOT statistically distinguishable from zero. The naive contaminated pooled contrast is +130.9%, dropping to +63.9% when cohort events are excluded. Of 5,419 treated launches, 382 (7.0%) had zero non-cohort buyers in the first 30 minutes. The author explicitly reports that the activity-matched placebo estimator is itself biased (median placebo lift +189.6%, above the real effect in 100/100 seeds) and retains it only as a bias diagnostic, not a falsification test.
findings.actionable_for_bot: This is a rigorous, honest quantification of the front-running problem in your exact market: coordinated early buyers add headcount but no measurable money. 'Lots of buyers in the first 30 minutes' is therefore a contaminated feature — split your participation-evidence metric into unique-buyer count AND non-cohort SOL inflow, and weight the latter. Anything that fires on buyer count alone is being farmed.

findings.claim: Coordinated bot mention campaigns are real and measurable — 61% bot-driven engagement — but the standard tool for detecting them no longer works
findings.detail: Saha Roy et al., 'Unveiling the Risks of NFT Promotion Scams' (arXiv:2301.09806): longitudinal study of 439 Twitter promotion accounts that promoted 823 unique projects over two months. 'more than 36% of these projects were fraudulent'. Sampling 100 retweeters per promotion tweet across 283,409 total users, at Botometer threshold t=0.43: 'more than 61% of users (n=173,446) who had retweeted promotion tweets exhibited bot-like activity.' By contrast '72.1% of all comments came from real accounts.' '46.2% of the NFT promotion accounts (n=203) had been suspended' over the study. Their own classifier flagged 382 new fraudulent projects at 95.2% TPR; those accounts had 'a median follower count of 3.7k and a median like count of 198 (based on the first 10 posts in their timeline)'. Enforcement was near-zero: 'only 59 out of 382 fraudulent NFT projects (approximately 15%) were suspended by Twitter within a week'. Losses in this modest sample exceeded $5.1 million. Botometer's public service is no longer operable following X's API repricing, so the t=0.43 threshold is not directly reproducible today.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Implementable proxy for the dead Botometer: for a token's mention set, compute (i) the fraction of distinct engaging accounts whose created_at is within 90 days, (ii) the fraction whose followers_count/followings_count < 0.1, (iii) the Jaccard overlap of engager sets across the last N tokens promoted by the same handle, (iv) near-duplicate text rate across mentions. The 'same accounts topping the PnL table on every promoted token' pattern that Bubblemaps used is the on-chain analogue of (iii) and is cheaper to compute. Median 3.7k followers / 198 likes on first 10 posts is a usable calibration point for what a scam-promoter profile looks like.

findings.claim: Detecting a repurposed/hacked X account: the reliable primitives are created_at, user_id stability, and profile-change events — not follower count
findings.detail: Mechanics verified from Sorsa's API docs: the User object exposes created_at (ISO 8601 account creation date) which does NOT change when a handle is repurposed, while GET /username-to-id notes 'Unlike usernames, user IDs never change.' The Follower object carries a follow date, so you can measure the age distribution of the follower cohort. SocialData's Monitoring API has a dedicated 'User Profile' monitor type that fires a webhook 'when profile information like bio or name' changes, ~30s latency, ~$4.99/month for up to 10 monitors. Bubblemaps' 'Hacked or Habits' case study on the Matt Furie account documents the real-world pattern: four tokens ($BOYZ, $MEGUSTA, $DORK, $MUFFIN) promoted within a single week in 2026, posts deleted with compromise claims, 'the same wallets tended to top the profit-and-loss tables on each promoted token', three compromises in one month with no security upgrade, location mismatches and extended prior inactivity, account went private afterward. Their conclusion was roughly 50-50 between genuine repeat compromise and insider involvement.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Concrete veto rule: reject when the token's advertised X handle satisfies (created_at older than 365 days) AND (the account's earliest crypto-related post is younger than 14 days) AND (a long posting gap exists in the timeline immediately before the crypto pivot). Add a hard reject when the same wallet cluster appears in the top-10 realised-PnL set for two or more tokens promoted by the same handle within 30 days — that is the strongest documented signature and it is on-chain, so it costs you nothing extra. Confidence is medium because no paper has measured the precision/recall of these rules at scale; they are pattern-matched from investigations, not validated.

findings.claim: Celebrity/KOL-called tokens: measured drawdowns of 93-98% and extraction concentrated in one cluster within an hour
findings.detail: $HAWK (Bubblemaps): launched 2024-12-04, peak market cap ~$500M, final ~$25M, 'roughly 98%' decline, collapse within days; '96% of the supply in one cluster' at TGE, '80%+ of the supply' retained by team, only '3%' sent to the Meteora LP pool; 285 presale investors with a 17% strategic allocation 'fully unlocked at TGE'; '155 wallets sold at least some of their bags' realising '$3.3M'. $LIBRA (Bubblemaps): announced by President Milei 2025-02-14, peak ~$4 billion in under two days, '82% cluster concentration', '$87 million in a single hour' extracted early on 2025-02-15 (148,343 SOL ≈ $29.6M; 69,275 SOL ≈ $13.8M; $42.79M USDC to a Squad Vault), '$25M in liquidity pool fees within one hour', investor losses exceeding $250 million; extraction was done by adding one-sided liquidity and pulling stables rather than by open-market selling, to avoid slippage. $TRUMP (peer-reviewed, SSRN 6479621): '93.4% decline from its all-time closing price high of $45.50 on January 19, 2025, to $3.00 on March 27, 2026'; two subsequent promotional events 'created temporary price spikes but did not reverse' the decline.
findings.actionable_for_bot: The biggest calls in history produced 93-98% drawdowns. Your laddered scale-out with cost recovery at 1.6x is the correct structural response; the LIBRA one-sided-liquidity extraction pattern is also a concrete detector — watch for single-sided LP adds and stable removals from the pool, which precede price collapse without printing a large sell.

findings.claim: 'First mention velocity' has no published predictive value for memecoins that I could find; the honest adjacent evidence is weak and slow
findings.detail: I searched arXiv (multiple query formulations), Crossref, and fetched every candidate paper. Nothing measures mention-velocity-to-return on memecoins. The nearest published results: (1) Alizadeh et al., arXiv:2411.05577 — LLM-extracted buy signals from crypto news outlets and influencers, VAR/Granger against the top nine cryptocurrencies: 'the results show a mixed pattern across cryptocurrencies and temporal periods. However, we found that for the top three cryptocurrencies... their aggregated LLM-detected trading signal over the preceding 24 hours granger-causes fluctuations in their market prices, exhibiting a lag of at least 6 hours.' Six hours, majors only, mixed. (2) 'Social Media Finfluencers: Evidence from YouTube and Cryptocurrencies' (SSRN 4594081): 'while aggregate new video counts on a specific cryptocurrency Granger-causes its price to increase the following day, new video counts by top finfluencers do not. Our evidence suggests that YouTube influencers do not directly influence cryptocurrency prices, but YouTube is likely a platform that propagates the herding behavior.' (3) Kropiunig et al., arXiv:2603.12000, 'Credibility Matters: Motivations, Characteristics, and Influence Mechanisms of Crypto Key Opinion Leaders' — 13 qualitative interviews, no return data whatsoever.
findings.actionable_for_bot: Do not ship a mention-velocity entry trigger and do not pay for a product that sells one as validated. If you want to know whether it works on your market, you already have the apparatus: log first-mention timestamp and mention counts alongside your existing 924-launch census schema, wait for a few thousand launches, and test it yourself against your measured base rates (median peak 1.000x, 7.5% ever 2x). That is a 2-3 month measurement, not a purchase.

findings.claim: Ecosystem-level base rates that bound how much any social signal can be worth
findings.detail: Chainalysis 2025 market-manipulation report: '2,063,519' tokens launched in 2024, '873,957' listed on a DEX ('42.54%'), '74,037' displaying pump-and-dump patterns ('3.59% of all launched tokens'); average time to abandonment 6.23 days, median 0 days, p90 8 days, p99 123 days; '94%' of rugged pools rugged by the deployer address, '6%' by funded addresses; only '1.7%' of launched tokens were actively traded within 30 days. Chainalysis 2024 report (Ethereum 2023): 'just over 370,000 tokens were launched', ~168,600 DEX-listed, '54.6% of tokens that were listed on a DEX' met three suspicious-pattern criteria (90,408 tokens, 24.4% of all launched), collectively '$241.6 million in profit in 2023' at 'just $2,672 each' per token; one address 'launched 81 different token types to generate an estimated $830,000'; these tokens were 'only 1.3% of total trade volume on Ethereum DEXes'. MemeChain (arXiv:2601.22185): 34,988 meme coins across Ethereum, BNB, Solana, Base; '1,801 tokens (5.15%) that cease all trading activity within just 24 hours of launch'.
findings.actionable_for_bot: $2,672 median scammer profit per token tells you the adversary's economics: they are running volume, not craft. That is why on-chain behavioral features generalise (the playbook is repetitive) and why social features do not (the narrative is disposable). Your own census (median peak 1.000x) is consistent with the 1.7%-actively-traded-at-30-days figure.

findings.claim: A 15-day live Solana deployment shows filter-stack results are structurally fragile at small sample sizes
findings.detail: Kamat, arXiv:2606.08232, 190 paper trades March 29 - April 12 2026: 40.5% win rate, mean per-trade +0.62%, cumulative +117.7% (net SOL +0.039), skewness -1.21, excess kurtosis 6.61. 'Removing the top three trades (1.6 percent of sample) flips cumulative return unprofitable.' Hour-of-day test: three worst hours (2, 13, 23 UTC; n=17, mean -11.60%) vs all others (n=173, mean +1.82%) gives Mann-Whitney U=1,345, p=0.5634, rank-biserial r=0.085 — 'directional and non-confirmatory'. Counterfactual rejection tracking: 4,874 forward observations across 184 rejection events; 'Of the 48 events observed for at least six hours, 27 (56.25 percent) reached a 50 percent drawdown from reference; the full-cohort figure of 17.9 percent is reported... as a censored lower bound.'
findings.actionable_for_bot: Directly transferable methodology: track the forward returns of tokens your filter REJECTS, not just the ones you buy. 56.25% of rejects hitting -50% within six hours is how you prove a filter is net-positive rather than assuming it. Also: at n<300 on a kurtosis-6.6 distribution, any A/B test of a social feature will be noise — pre-commit to a sample size before you evaluate whether X data helped.
